nameStory: Chicita's Sea Storm Lichen honors a lichenologist named Chicita, though the 'Sea Storm' part of the name comes from its genus Cetrelia, which refers to the lichen's ability to weather intense conditions. Like a ship riding out ocean storms, this hardy lichen clings to its rocky and woody homes through New England's harsh winters and humid summers.
description: Chicita's Sea Storm Lichen is a leafy, foliose lichen that forms spreading patches on tree bark and mossy rocks. Its thin, overlapping lobes create a lettuce-like appearance that can spread several inches across over many years. The lichen has a distinctive grayish-green color when dry that becomes more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy patches with thin, overlapping lobes that feel papery and delicate to the touch, like tissue paper that's been slightly dampened

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green when dry, becoming a brighter, more vibrant green when wet - the color change is quite dramatic after rain

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on both mossy rocks and tree trunks, often preferring spots where moisture lingers longer

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth and slightly waxy, while the underside is typically darker with small root-like structures called rhizines

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can grow 2-4 inches across, with lobes extending outward in an irregular, somewhat circular pattern

habitat: Look for Chicita's Sea Storm Lichen in moist, shaded areas of New England's forests, particularly on deciduous trees like maples and oaks, as well as on moss-covered boulders and rock outcrops. It prefers locations with consistent humidity, such as north-facing slopes, stream valleys, and areas with good canopy cover that stay damp longer after rain.

seasonality.spring: Easy to spot when vibrant green from frequent spring rains. New growth begins as temperatures warm, though growth is extremely slow.
seasonality.summer: Often appears grayish and less noticeable during dry spells, but rainstorms bring out the bright green coloration that makes identification easier.
seasonality.fall: Color changes with moisture become more pronounced as humidity fluctuates. Wet autumn days provide excellent viewing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round, appearing more grayish-brown against snow and bark. Ice and snow can make the texture more brittle temporarily.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 8 times by citizen scientists and researchers - making each discovery a genuine treasure hunt victory that contributes valuable data to our understanding of lichen distribution!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative Sea Storm Lichen (Cetrelia olivetorum), but Chicita's tends to have more delicate, thinner lobes and often grows in slightly different microhabitats. When in doubt, note the exact substrate and take photos - these subtle differences matter for these uncommon species.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Cetrelia can be tricky to pronounce (seh-TREE-lee-ah), and these lichens are part of the shield lichen family, though they don't form the typical shield-shaped reproductive structures as commonly as their relatives do.
compareHints: Compared to Sea Storm Lichen (Cetrelia olivetorum), Chicita's Sea Storm Lichen typically has more delicate, thinner lobes and may show subtle differences in color intensity when wet. Both species are quite rare in New England, so any Cetrelia discovery is noteworthy and worth documenting carefully with photos and location data.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sea Storm Lichen differs from its close relative Chicita's Sea Storm Lichen primarily in subtle chemical characteristics that require laboratory testing to distinguish.
